reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: Thin basement membrane nephropathy typically causes persistent or intermittent isolated microscopic haematuria, often discovered incidentally and frequently familial
It is usually associated with heterozygous variants in the type IV collagen genes COL4A3 or COL4A4, placing it at the mild end of the Alport spectrum
The defining feature on electron microscopy is diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane without the lamellation seen in classic Alport syndrome
Blood pressure, renal function and proteinuria are characteristically normal, and the traditional term benign familial haematuria reflects the usually favourable course
Hearing and eyes are typically unaffected, in contrast to Alport syndrome
Because carriers of COL4A3/COL4A4 variants can occasionally develop proteinuria, hypertension or progressive disease, long-term monitoring is prudent
Family screening and genetic counselling help distinguish it from progressive autosomal Alport disease within the same gene family
reference.pathophysiology: Thin basement membrane nephropathy is a disorder of the type IV collagen network that forms the glomerular basement membrane. Heterozygous variants in COL4A3 or COL4A4, which encode alpha chains of type IV collagen, produce a structurally thinner but largely functional basement membrane. The attenuated membrane is more permeable to red cells, giving rise to persistent glomerular (dysmorphic) microscopic haematuria, but in most people the filtration barrier otherwise functions normally so proteinuria, hypertension and renal impairment are absent or minimal. Because the same genes, when affected biallelically or with certain variants, cause autosomal recessive or dominant Alport syndrome, the condition represents the mild end of a continuous type IV collagen disease spectrum, and a minority of carriers show slow progression over decades.
additionalDifferentials: Alport syndrome (X-linked or autosomal, with progressive disease and extrarenal features)
Urological (non-glomerular) causes of haematuria such as stones or tumours
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and phase-contrast microscopy to confirm glomerular (dysmorphic) red cells
Quantification of proteinuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine or protein-to-creatinine ratio)
Renal function and blood pressure monitoring over time
Family history and screening of relatives for haematuria
Audiometry and ophthalmological review to exclude Alport features when indicated
Kidney biopsy with electron microscopy, or genetic testing of COL4A3/COL4A4, when the diagnosis or prognosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rising blood pressure or declining renal function
Hearing loss or ocular abnormalities suggesting Alport syndrome
Family history of end-stage kidney disease
Visible (macroscopic) or non-glomerular haematuria requiring urological evaluation
reference.prognosis: The great majority of individuals maintain normal renal function lifelong with isolated haematuria, but because COL4A3/COL4A4 carriers occasionally progress, ongoing surveillance for proteinuria, hypertension and renal decline is warranted.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition entirely benign and discharging without any follow-up
Failing to recognise it as part of the Alport type IV collagen spectrum
Overlooking a urological cause when haematuria is non-glomerular or visible
Not screening the family or offering genetic counselling
Missing early extrarenal features that would reclassify the patient as having Alport syndrome
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Expert consensus guidance on Alport spectrum / type IV collagen disorders
management: No disease-specific drug therapy is needed for isolated glomerular microscopic haematuria; provide reassurance and avoid nephrotoxic agents
Introduce renin-angiotensin blockade with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker only if proteinuria or hypertension develops
Periodically monitor blood pressure, urinary protein quantification and renal function to detect the minority who progress along the type IV collagen spectrum
Screen first-degree relatives for haematuria and offer clinical-genetics counselling given the heritable COL4A3/COL4A4 basis
Arrange audiometry and ophthalmological review if extrarenal features raise the possibility of Alport syndrome
Refer to nephrology and escalate investigation (biopsy or COL4A3/COL4A4 genetic testing) if proteinuria, hypertension or declining renal function emerge
